game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

review_text_raw: I think Orwell as a game is a great concept, but could have been executed far better. The game highlights important information, and railroads you into making choices that aren't backed by evidence. It doesn't provide enough detail for you to make judgement calls, but leaves you between two equally plausible answers, and forces you to make a choice. A better way of doing this would have been to present more information than necessary, and let players sort out what's important, and take their own notes. I would have preferred the game to involve less bias - letting players make their own choices, and come to their own conclusion on the benefits - or invasions - of government surveillance. I also feel the ending was robbed from me. I simply couldn't figure out how to support the cause of Thought, and wanted to have to face the ethical dilemma of doing so. Instead, I had to give them in as the only way to move forward. I really wanted to like this game, but I ultimately can't recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
With "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" Osmotic Studios and publisher Daedalic Entertainment deliver a narrative surveillance thriller that quietly turns its own core theme into self parody. The player is asked to watch over the privacy of others, while in the background a telemetry chain made of Steam, Unity and Mailchimp wakes up, of which not a single word can be found on the product page.

[h1]What does the product do?[/h1]On first launch the game already talks to Steam, fetches the SDR config for AppID 491950. In parallel Unity reaches out to Google Cloud, generates a persistent userid and ships a full hardware profile. Only after all of this does the player see a brief in game pointer to an external privacy notice.

[h1]Who operates the product?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH (formerly Fellow Traveller)
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH (current publisher)

[h1]Which service providers are involved?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH
Valve Corporation
Unity Technologies
Google, LLC (infrastructure for Unity)
Intuit Mailchimp (owned by Intuit Inc.)
[noparse]Amazon.com, Inc.[/noparse]

[h1]What data is collected?[/h1]
Unique identifiers have been redacted for the review.
[b]Unity Analytics (no visible notice)[/b]
Unity 6000.3.8f1 fires POST requests to the Unity Analytics config and event endpoints. The endpoints resolve to Google Cloud in the United States.
[list][*] Persistent userid and deviceid, sessionid, session_count
[*] appid and build_guid
[*] Full hardware profile: CPU, RAM, VRAM, GPU vendor, driver, D3D12 feature level
[*] OS version, language, mainboard model, machine hostname
[*] Events appStart, appStop, SubsystemInfo, shaderRuntimeInfo
[/list]No OptIn is shown, tracking cannot be turned off inside the game.

[b]Steam Datagram Relay[/b]
The client fetches the Steam SDR configuration for the game and then opens 34 UDP connections to Frankfurt, Stockholm, London, Paris, Vienna, Warsaw, Amsterdam, New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Seattle, Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Mumbai, Sydney, Johannesburg and Dubai. For a pure single player thriller this fanout provides no benefit.

[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
The in game newsletter sends first name, email and the tag "Orwell" straight to the Mailchimp REST API. The client uses a fixed HTTP Basic Auth credential baked into the build, "user:[redacted]-us14", which is a full Mailchimp API key visible in any network capture. The server response leaks list metadata, sender, statistics and a contact address (Papenstrasse 27, 22089 Hamburg) that differs from the one in the privacy notice. Headers reveal hosting in AWS us east 2.

[h1]GDPR violations in detail[/h1]
[b]Unity Analytics without consent[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)a Transparency: Transmission starts before the user is informed
[*] Art. 6 Lawfulness: No consent, no documented legitimate interest
[*] Art. 7 Consent: No OptIn dialog, the pointer arrives too late
[*] Art. 13 Information obligation: Unity Analytics and Google Cloud are not named
[*] Art. 25 Privacy by Design: Tracking is default, no in game switch
[*] Art. 44ff Third country transfer: US Google Cloud, no SCC notice in game
[/list]
[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)f Integrity: The API key sits in plain text in the game binary
[*] Art. 13: Hosting in the US is not disclosed in game
[*] Art. 25: No server side email validation
[*] Art. 44ff: Third country transfer to the US, no visible safeguard
[/list]
[b]Steam SDR[/b]
Art. 5(1)c Data minimization: 34 worldwide relays for a solo title are excessive.

[h1]Privacy policy and Opt-in/Opt-out[/h1]
The Steam product page does not show or link any privacy policy or EULA. Inside the game a short pointer appears during profile creation, but only after Steam SDR and Unity have already shipped data abroad. The Steam age rating in Germany is "12 and up" while the Osmotic privacy notice itself requires a minimum age of 18. No age verification takes place.

A second oversight: the in game privacy notice is supposed to exist in English and German. In reality the "German" file is a word for word copy of the English text, only the headline reads "Datenschutzerklärung". A German speaking user has no proper localized notice available in game, which under Art. 12 GDPR is a serious flaw.

The notice itself does not name Unity Analytics, does not mention the Google Cloud infrastructure, does not list the Mailchimp pipeline and says nothing about a hardcoded API key inside the client.

[h1]Can this behavior be blocked?[/h1]
Yes, largely. The Unity Analytics endpoints, the Mailchimp REST API and the Steam SDR config request can all be blocked at the network layer without breaking gameplay. "Orwell" is a pure single player title, neither Unity Analytics nor SDR are required for it to run.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" stages a surveillance state and trains the player to quietly oversee the data of strangers, while at the same time keeping a close eye inside its own engine room.

The Steam product page skips any data protection or EULA information, the in game pointer arrives too late and in a language version that is German only by name. Unity Analytics runs without a visible OptIn through Google Cloud in the United States, the newsletter pipeline goes through Mailchimp with an API key baked into the client, and Steam SDR opens 34 UDP connections worldwide for a solo title.

The thematic punch line lands twice here, once in the script and once in the network log.

[h1]Additional Info[/h1]
Additional details, including a full connection overview for blocking access, involved IPv4 addresses, company information and the German version of the review, are available as usual at [url=https://gameindustry.eu]GameIndustry[/url]. If you're interested, join the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/penguindome]Penguin Domination[/url] group to stay informed about new reviews on Steam.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's borderline but I'd lean towards no.

Effectively choose your own adventure, with the agency being 'what you leave out' by not reporting it to the agency.
The problem is some things are required to be reported to move the plot forward, and those aren't marked in any special way. Thus, there were a few times where I just started reporting everything, even if I wanted to leave it out.

Additionally, the plot anded up being "mass surveillance is bad" (obviously given the title), but by being "reports everything" robot, I caught two mass murderers, and wasted one innocent person's time in jail for a few days. Then I was lectured by a mass murderer and an anti-government hacker for 5 minutes, while waiting for the police to take the murderer away.

Somehow the terrible writing has pushed me more towards being pro surveillance lol.

Finally, it's really short (3hr), but I got it for 6 bucks, so I think I got my money's worth.

Overall like I said really borderline, but I wouldn't recommend it to most people.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]!

This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.

What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? 

The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game.

So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]! This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label. What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close. What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game. So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Interesting, compelling, and flawed. Contrary to some negative reviews I don't mind the format of Orwell being a linear visual novel, sometimes the best way to tell a complicated story is to tell it simply, and for what it's worth, it works well as long as Orwell is telling the story it thinks it is. 

With that being said, Orwell pulls its biggest punch on its lynchpin issue concerning its closing question on a terrorist attack you've been investigating from the beginning of the story, where, when circling back at the climax, Orwell thinks it's asking you a sensible question. Would I condemn the use of Orwellian nation state surveillance in the face of what we've learned during the story? 

Of course it's something I condemn, we've all a right to privacy.

But in order to answer the question as Orwell wants to phrase it, i found myself being really frustrated with how the game allows you to give your answer, and i'm really disappointed with what feels like really negligent storytelling. 

Orwell isnt as mature as it thinks it is. At the crux of it, Orwell isn't asking you to measure freedom against safety, It asks would you rather be a bootlicker to solve a terror attack killing several and wounding others, or let the perpetrators off because the developers skipped watching minority report?

We've a right to live free from terror, and the real fault of Orwell is that it ends up presenting terror and surveillance as equivalent issues rather than being in tension with one another. You're not asked what would you be willing to do to prevent an act of terror, it's already happened, people have died.

That Orwell also asks if you would like to give the system a middle finger by way of a Watergate sidestep to, again, apprehending conspirators / co-conspirators to a terror attack seems to be completely missing the point.

Am I missing things and details here? Almost certainly, there are a few different endings and granular differences depending on your choices throughout the story that paint a different picture. But for me, Orwell treats 1984 as the only book on the shelf.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've been hesitating writing a review for this one, as part of me likes the game but another part is very annoyed with it. After giving it some rest and extra thought, I have to downvote it.

The gameplay is fine, I actually quite liked that. The concept works and I would have loved a much more difficult version using this technique.

Sadly, the story is very flawed and made in such a way to get the game's "message" out. It is very biased towards why all this is a bad idea and pretty much gives no indication why and how it could actually work. And you know, that all would have been fine if done right, but everything in the story hinges on a lot of coincidences and it takes away from how an actual Orwell system could maybe properly work.

It still wouldn't, but this case does not show the actual flaws of such a system. And that is the problem of this game. It starts off by you following ONE suspect. In a true case you would have had information on everyone at the crime scene, and this is only the first big flaw why this is a bad representation of a system like this. [spoiler]And then that suspect ends up not being involved at all, but by coincidence she does happen to be in contact with the true criminal. Oh, sure, the writers eventually tried to make a link and explain it was the criminal who was responsible for the first suspect to be a the crime scene. Which ends up with the story making even less sense as there is absolutely no indication why the criminal would even want this suspect to be at the first crime scene.[/spoiler] And it just goes downhill from there, with more random stuff happening that just happens to be convenient for this poor mirror or a true spying system.

Conclusion: Good concept, but the writing keeps it from being a good game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

ディストピアの監視システムを用いる調査官という導入は凄く面白いし実際に惹き込まれましたが、幾つかの要素が引っ掛かって最終的に「惜しいな」という感想に着地しました。

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。
更に、二次的な関係者(直接の監視対象ではない人々)の情報には触れられず、例えば誰かの両親や友人等が相関図に載っても飽くまで賑やかしで、RPGで言うなら「目的地周辺だけ作ってあるマップ」みたいな印象を受けるので没入感を削がれます。
そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

物語や世界観についても引っ掛かります。国民の情報がOrwellに登録されておらず、住所も電話番号も全てプレイヤーが探し出す事になるのは、ゲーム内での事案がOrwellの初陣であるにせよ監視社会のディストピアを念頭に置くなら中途半端な気がしますし、基本的な個人情報から調査となると手順に警察の捜査との差異も感じられません。
Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。
正直なところ、この作品がOrwellに在る社会構造を否定的に描いているのか肯定的に描いているのか判然としませんでした。

実績や細かい分岐の確認に改めてプレイしていたら印象も変わるのかもしれませんが、ここでシステム面が障害に。というのも、だいぶのんびりしたプレイで全5章終わらせるのに約4時間掛かったのですが、Orwellには台詞送りやスキップ機能がなく、更には選択に修正が効かない仕様なのでリプレイへの精神的なハードルが高いです。
台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

A lot of people are praising this game, but it's really simple. There are very few choices with usually obvious consiquences.

Most of the game feels like work. You click and drag the things that are highlighted and then the guy reveals more plot points and gives you more documents to read while you click and drag more stuff. It's made all the more painful by false "upload" times (really? Uploading text to the most complex security system ever takes 3+ seconds each time!? I understand people are interested in the story, or the greater point about surveillance, but as a game, this is just too simple. For a far better experience with a similar concept, I would highly suggest the ARG "This House Has People In It"

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: Don't bother, you're basically just a human web-crawler.

This game completely misses the point of what Orwellian infrastructure would look like in the first place and does everything in its power to not allow you any information at all. This game has no right to call itself Orwell, it has nothing to do with surveillance. Yea you have access to data, but the constant opinionated non-rational commentary by the "Adviser" undermines the whole of it. I can't of course claim the outcome wouldn't be the same in an actually Orwellian policy, but it sure as hell shouldn't look like this. In no way am I defending Orwellian values either, but their implementation here is.. well it isn't. It's just not there.
When choose information to be considered, the information changes between the point where you drag it from and the actual information recorded. 
The UI is unintuitive and very hard to navigate. The artificial load times don't help either, from both the gameplay loop and story-telling perspective, they make no sense.

Just to blow of some steam about how disappointed I am in this game, I'll address a couple reviews:

“Grabs the problem of how we balance our own liberty and our safety and turns it into a thrilling adventure.” 9/10 – Polygon
It does make a feeble attempt at tackling the problem of balancing safety and liberty, but fails miserably. Not only does it not represent what you could call Orwellian infrastructure, it doesn't even try. Access to information is limited and the information itself misinterpreted. Your "superior" is clearly opinionated, easily influenced and not of very high deductive capacity. Hardly a "thrilling adventure", the pace of the game is dictated by the game, not by the player. You can't move fast, despite the game making constant remarks about how you should. Nothing about this is thrilling, it's a very slow burner, except it isn't good. It's attempting to show flaws in Orwellian policies but fails to represent them, only showing flaws in its own design.

“A harrowing look into a reality where Big Brother is always watching” Rock Paper Shotgun
The only "harrowing" thing about this game is how it managed to get out of indev. The UI of this game is atrocious in both mechanical as well as logical sense. Mechanically navigating anywhere in this game is a pain in the bum, and the game punishes you every time you try to make more than 1 action per 10 seconds. The whole bit about conflicting data chunks is just stupid. First of all it should have a dating mechanism in the data collection software, which would prevent 90% of the data chunk conflicts in the first place. Secondly, why bother trying to pick one out of the 2 conflicting data points when all you're doing is presenting to someone who can clearly barely tie their own shoe-laces, much less decide outcomes for other people. I wouldn't let this "Adviser" choose the color of desktop background, much less my or anyone else's legal standing. Oh and did I mention: You can't go back on whatever the "Adviser" was saying either, so tough luck if you wanted to submit 2 pieces of information and started navigating before you can notice the Adviser popping up on screen, immediately skipping possibly vital dialog.

“In an age where so much personal information is willingly released by so many, Orwell brilliantly explores the implications of this data being misinterpreted.” 8/10 – GameSpot
This. That's the exact problem with the game, there isn't supposed to be an interpretation to be done in the first place. At the start of the game, you're presented with the job of a data-gatherer. It's not up to you to interpret this data and neither should it be up to the "Adviser". Not just because his brain activity matches that of a fork, but because he simply does not have all the data. Neither does the player, nobody does. Once the information is conclusive all on it's own and only then should there be an attempt at interpretation. It's a simple rational analysis up until then. Or at least it should've been. Instead the game constantly pedals it's own point with forced story-telling.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I feel a bit bad about giving a poor review for a game I received for free, especially since the game is doing a lot of things right. Even so, at the end of the day, I just didn't find the motivation to continue playing this game. It has a distinctive art style, is tackling pressing societal issues, and isn't expensive. Gameplay-wise, however, I'm being force-fed documents with the important parts already highlighted. I move these things to a profile, and continue my journey. As I learn more about the person I'm investigating, I'm nevertheless unable to take things back that proved false or misleading. Conclusions based on my findings are left with the NPCs, so in the end, I'm just finding and selecting pieces of information. Maybe that's a solid dystopian view of surveillance in the future, but it wasn't too much fun as a game, at least not for me.

I would compare it to Black Mirror's "The Waldo Moment" episode. I appreciate what it's trying to say, but it isn't said in a compelling way.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The problem I have with this game is that it tries to hold you accountable for choices you did not make. Your task in Orwell is simply to retrieve information, someone will make a decision based on the information you collect. However, you are not in control of when this person makes a decision, so at times your attempt to gather all information to get the full picture are halted midway.  In addition, you are forced to choose between information chunks at crucial moments in the game even though there is no reason why you should. By doing so, the game forces you to not consider the entire context. And what does the game do to you at end? Blame you for not considering the entire context.

Another problem I have with this game is the more philosophical debate of an Orwellian surveillance system. By pretending that there is no separation of power or strict legislation on how evidence may be gathered, the creators abuse the fictive setting to criticize such a system. Yes, such a system would be horrible in certain dictatorship countries that currently exist, but we already know that don't we? It's an interesting concept that can be used for good as well. This nuance is missing in the story and as a result the writers and this game discredit themselves as a worthy piece of fiction.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lot of good, but outweighed by the bad.

The game was entertaining and built on a thought-provoking premise, but the game is far too short (roughly four hours in length) and the premise of the game loses its edge when the game picks a side on the question if society should sacrifice privacy for security instead of leaving that decision up to the player.

The story is well-written but offers very little in replayability. The games premise would have room for several scenarios where the player has to puzzle together what has happened or attempt to prevent crimes from happening, placing the player in situations where he has to weigh his decision how deep into someones private-life he should go to discover the truth, and even then be left with an uncertainty that forces him to make decisions based only his own interpretation of the truth. Instead, the game presents one scenario that plays out over a five-day period. The game-mechanics themselves are not complicated and the games graphics and presentation is mostly text and still-pictures, so more scenarios should not be difficult or time-consuming to add later on.

If the game had more meat on the bones I would recommend it, but for the moment this is a brief game with little replayability, but potential for a lot more.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wish I liked it because on the paper it's 100% a game for me but I'm forced to admit I just don't.

First of all it's not detective work, you just drop pieces of information in a database hoping it makes the story progress.

Because you're not technically forced to drop all the information in the database, you quickly try to have an impact on the story's progression by keeping some info to yourself, but the story only progresses when specific info is used and you never know which info is necessary or not so you can't really make informed choices on what to give Orwell and what to not.

I quickly find myself stuck with the story not progressing because I've decided to keep a piece of information that's mandatory for the story to continue and so I have to start from the top and review everything which is tedious and drop random bits of information I've kept until I find the one that was necessary for the story to continue which means I really can't choose what I keep or don't keep,

or I straight up give all the info away from the start to not have to review everything later once I'm stuck which again means I can't choose what I keep or don't keep.

There seems to be a system of highlighting the files where there still is relevant information but I don't understand how it works. Sometimes files are highlighted and there's nothing left on them and sometimes they aren't highlighted and there's still important things on them. It's very confusing.

I also suspect the political messaging of the game is really not so subtle and just "violence is bad" with no nuance but I can't tell you for sure because I'm too frustrated with the gameplay to go to the end of the story at this point. My other issue with the writing that I just can't seem to get over is that it makes zero sense that people who are fighting surveillance would post on the internet about it with their full name and photo or extremely basic aliases. Not posting about your actions on the internet is activism 101.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more.

I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An amazing concept, but the result is disappointing.
1) You do not investigate. You search documents for highlighted clues that you may upload into an investigation database. And you cannot delete them when they turn out to be misleading. Naturally i was careful not to upload dubious claims. Wrong. That gets you stuck. Orwel thrives on rumours, you have to upload these to get new related documents.

2) The writing is boring. The rudimentary gameplay wouldn't matter if the writing was fresh, but the documents you have to go through are as boring as real corporate websites and random people's blogs. Add an annoying coworker and you start regretting you have got that job.

3) The game only pretends to tackle complex issues of privacy and security. The Government is a classical dystopian government that can and will prosecute on "suggestive evidence" which can easily be an off-hand remark of a third party taken out-of-context. If you do not like that, you can side with bomb-throwing anarchists. No third option though, so either way there will be bad outcomes. And that is why surveillance is bad, or so the logic goes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1][i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye One You’s[/i] centrism recklessly justifies surveillance[/h1]

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] (Osmotic Studios, 2016) should not have to prove that mass surveillance is a public danger. Lifting the name of one of the 20th century’s most enduring authors, [i]Orwell[/i] reverses the traditional dystopian power dynamic by casting the player as an investigator utilizing government software to snoop on anyone deemed potentially dangerous to the state. The setup is almost too clean to be proper satire, too on the nose to spark the outrage necessary to criticize what is fast becoming a common aspect of life.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality.

[i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination.

Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged.

But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power.

In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving.

The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance.

This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case?

[i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it.

Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down.

///

review_text_raw:
I don't feel like I can truly call this a detective game, or even a puzzle game. The choices available are limited (2-3 outcomes), and [spoiler] almost none of the choices that are made throughout the game affect the ending, or really the flow of the story in general[/spoiler]. Choices do not matter. [spoiler] Speaking of the ending, I felt that they were quite sudden, especially "Thoughts are free", and didn't follow entirely plausibly from the actions you took to get there. How exactly does the investigator incriminating oneself IMMEDIATELY result in the termination of Orwell? How does an incredibly sophisticated surveillance program like Orwell, even still in test phase, get torn down in a day? Never mind that there were probably backup investigators lined up, or that The Party likely would not have wanted to let go of the project so easily. If the main message of the story is that "surveillance cannot be impartial and bias will always be present", then it seems careless to throw away the secondary message - "surveillance is pervasive and nigh impossible to detect and curtail once it reaches a tipping point" - in the final moment. And yet curtail in an instant, they did. [/spoiler]

Credit where it is due, the character dialogue and writings felt very genuine, and portrayed each person convincingly.

Other reviewers have already said all of this, better. Like [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/MangoMaraudr/recommended/491950/]this one[/url].

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I hesitated before giving the thumb down to a game which is not completely bad, but definitely not for everyone.
The game basically plays like a visual story where you have to grab (drag  & drop more exactly) chunks of data to the left of the screen on the right character, the interface is not perfect (no right clicking to add intel faster, some back buttons are just visuals). The game is SLOW and a bit boring if you play in one go, no way to speed up text, no voice acting, forces you to wait on a few occasions. 
The writing isn't bad but characters lack personnality (bit shallow, not enough background), the game forces you to go one way and lacks some imaginative gameplay (older games would have make you work with visual clues, make interrogation yourself but Orwell keeps making you reading text). The problem is that it plays like a slow VN where you have to constantly look for the next button without any way to speed things up. 
It's not overly long but it feels long and the whole debate it's supposed to bring up falls a bit flat, also you can guess the "responsible person" before the end as soon as some intel is revealed. 
The game offers several ends but does not warn you before making the final choice (it did force you to watch a wall of text on an ugly colored screen before though) and would force you to replay from scratch to make another choice.

Don't mistaken me, those who are in for a lengthy text experience set in the modern world with text centered spying are in for a treat but it's definitely not for everyone.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's really hard for me to determine whether I do or don't recommend this, as I'm right on the line. I think overall, though, I have to lean into not recommending it.

The game starts off really well, with a really balanced juxtaposition of people being concerned about privacy versus the very real result of what you're able to accomplish through spying, really highlighting the blurred line between privacy and security. Further, the fact that there are rules in place - such as you can't hack someone without what is essentially a warrant from higher up in the system - makes it feel more grounded, and honestly like a more fair system. 

However, as you reach the end of the game, this completely falls apart. In the closing act, you get beaten around the head with the game designers' opinion, which is a very black-and-white "spying bad, privacy good", which entirely undermines the nuance the entire game up until that point had executed so well. I'll save the spoiler-filled rant for the end.

In addition to this, the gameplay has some glaring flaws. There are certain pieces of information that you absolutely [i]must[/i] collect to move forward, which is sometimes information that seems completely irrelevant (and you're outright told not to submit irrelevant information), forcing you to comb through every possible source with a fine-toothed comb, and sometimes just guess what they want you to submit.

Also, you can only extract verbatim phrases to submit, devoid of any context or clarification. Often, this leads to bizarre interpretations from the game. Like, apparently the game makers think [spoiler]that Depression or PTSD are things that make someone dangerous, rather than being a potentially debilitating disability[/spoiler]. Or perhaps you want to flag one piece of information because of it's context, but because that context isn't part of the auto-selected snippet, the game completely misinterprets it. For example, [spoiler]one girl is in a relationship with a guy, and helps herself to his wallet to make a couple purchases. Any reasonable person would have enough context to say, "Oh, she's borrowing his wallet, and he's only mildly annoyed that she's spending a lot? Clearly they are in a very serious relationship." How about the game? "She took his wallet? She has a history of theft! She's clearly a criminal!"[/spoiler] Like, wtf?

So that's why I just can't recommend this game. Despite the promise it shows, it really undermines itself, especially in the final stretch.

Now, about that endgame rant... Endgame spoilers follow: [spoiler]You reach the end of the game, and basically get lectured at by someone who (1) organized multiple bombings that killed dozens of people, (2) lied to and manipulated multiple friends to do her dirty work, ruining their lives, and (3) is completely unrepentant (going with the "can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs" excuse). What's worse, is that she did all this to protest the whole mass-spying thing, but the only reason you're even spying on anyone in that community is because of the bombings! Literally, she created the problem that she's complaining about.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Meanwhile, you (potentially) used [i]your[/i] minor sin of spying to save dozens or even hundreds of lives at the mall [i]she[/i] tried to bomb - targeting civilians to make people care more about her message. She also blames you for sending police in who end up killing her friend, just because, you know, they actually [i]were[/i] guilty of setting bombs to kill people, and opened fire on the police. How dare those cops return fire on a known bomber who is armed and dangerous just because she shot first![/spoiler]

[spoiler]And what's worse, is that all the other people involved in the plot-device-conference-call at the end [i]take her side![/i] Like, [i]really?[/i] In the end, you're basically pushed to take down the entire system you've been a part of, despite the fact that the game shows it doing an objectively good job of keeping people safe and bringing conspiracies to justice, because spying is bad, just, end of story, just take our word for that.[/spoiler]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
More of an immersive novel than a game, Orwell begins as a smart and thoroughly engaging experience that accurately captures the dilemma of state surveillance: The violation of privacy is bad and comes with risk, but there are still real threats that motivated the imposition of surveillance in the first place. Within this context, the events of Orwell are situated within "The Nation" - a hypothetical highly developed country saddled with all of the assets and burdens of the U.S., France, the U.K. or any similar nation. Osmotic deserves praise here - they tightly and intelligently create a nuanced setting without overburdening the player.

But the success doesn't last.

As the game progresses, Orwell begins to exhibit a grasping take on modern security that feels naive. The moderated presentation that offered a balanced dialectic fades, and the political messaging of the developers becomes increasingly heavy handed and blunt. None of this occurs in a way that is surprising or unique within the context of the public surveillance debate, it is only disappointing that they couldn't have done better.

In terms of technical game mechanics, while Orwell's gameplay is a slick, engrossing and well-crafted experience - the buyer should not expect any replay value outside of a 3-5 hour playthrough.

Leaving a negative review feels somewhat harsh, although within the context of a 91% positive title, it feels appropriate for balance. It is by no means a bad game - only one that fell frustratingly short of its potential.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: While the concept of the game is interesting I think it's not executed very well. Often times the game gets into a state where you can't collect any more information and you need to provide the surveillance system with data that you found. But there would often be two conflicting datasets, usually diametrically opposite, available for upload but you have no real way of determining which one is true/false. So you end up just taking the best guess and then the game starts playing this dramatic music because it's exactly at that point that somebody has to suddenly make a phone call or send an email with some sort of a revelation. Needless to say most of the time it doesn't land for me. My reaction to these situations would mostly be: "Oh, ok. I guess that's what happened.". The game goes out of its way to put you in a dead-end situation that could go either way and then it tries to make a tense situation out of it. It doesn't really work for me and I felt like the writing wasn't very strong in general. Especially when it comes to one character that communicates directly with you and beats you over the head with expository information and game tips in a way that attempts to be subtle but isn't really.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is a "profession simulator" style interactive novel where you control a privacy invading government employee, reading peoples emails and watching security cameras.  You're forced to make decisions to progress the story, although in a bit of hamfisted design, the developers obscure a lot of the readily available information you would have just to make the game more "interesting". 

The game is a very dry computer operation simulator where you're stuck using a fake web browser to plod through the tedious game, copying text and clicking on this and that.   I'm sure there's a "watching paint dry" simulator on Steam and it would be just as engaging.  Bonus points for the sheer irony of a game about big brother asking you for your email address so they can spam you and collect data on you.  That kind of dodginess is completely reprehensible, so even if the game was actually any good, I still wouldn't recommend it to make sure the developers are getting the message.

review_text_raw:
While the core concept is interesting, the game play and plot leave much to be desired. It is also incredibly short. The TLDR is that I would not recommend this unless the concept really grabs you.

The story revolves around a bombing and the activist group linked to it. You take the role of an investigator using social media, private messages/files and recorded phone calls to get to the bottom of everything. There seem to be a few possible different outcomes which could be interesting to explore if the people involved weren't so... stupid. I wont spoil anything but they basically make their own problems and then make bigger problems for themselves because they incorrectly think the bigger problems will solve their problems. It's like watching a train wreck in slow motion. It can be hard to get invested when you can't relate or empathise with the characters. I found myself thinking that most of them were horrible people who deserved what the plot threw at them.

The game play consists of reading through documents and chat logs and dragging over information that you determine to be relevant to the case. Some of this information is incorrect or contradictory and so you must vet information before committing it to the system. There are no taking information back even if you find contradicting information later on. This means a lot of your time will be spent going back and forward between different documents to pick out information and drag it to the appropriate file. This isn't exactly the most invigorating game play but when you are in the zone it can be somewhat enjoyable.

There isn't really much else to say. The game does have a political agenda and a underlying moral to it but it kind of falls on its face to the extent that I started to wonder if the resistant reading was the intended one.

There are multiple endings, and just to get one is very confusing because it feels like every possible ending is being thrown at you and you have to pick one. I already forced myself to finish one, and I don't think I will launch this game again.

Overall, if you're looking for a small investigation game or want to feel like a detective, pass on this game. It would have been a great mobile game, but is tedious on PC.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

I wrote this review on a whim after re-reading 1984, but to be sure I was assessing the game fairly I replayed the first couple of "days" (levels). I think my impressions are still accurate, and the game is still not worth playing. So on the one hand, at least the game is memorable. On the other:

In a word (one of George Orwell's own, suitably enough) the game is 'doubleplusungood'. It has very little to do with the author except for the state-surveillance meme - which was, in the first place, only "the tutorial" of 1984 - so that the game seems reluctant to explore or understand its own namesake. This is more noticeable in the sequel, which is less interested in recreating the horrifying Newspeak of 1984 ("we shall make thoughtcrime [ideological dissension] literally impossible, because there will be no words in which to express it") so much as awkwardly recreating the contemporary and vapid phenomena of 'fake news narratives'. It's cheaply political, far from the surgical satire with which George condemned his contemporary socialists, or the Isaianic fury with which he condemned the whole politically progressive enterprise. All told, the devs would have been better off writing an essay on 1984 than making two (soon to be three, I hear) shoddy video game adaptations; but should they direct their talents to original systems and concepts, I strongly believe they can make a playable game.
