game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Short game with an interesting concept; that, in my opinion, failed to deliver. For the most part, the game does a good job keeping you guessing if you are making the right choices; but overall, I found the game boring and kept playing only to finish the story, just to be disappointed.

The entire gameplay loop consists of reading and dragging sentences from the right side of the screen to the left. Depending on your choices, the story can move in slightly different directions.

The story was interesting enough to keep me playing. You are an investigator working for a government surveillance system trying to unravel a terrorist group. The game wants you to deal with all the moral struggle that comes with invading people's privacy, but I think the premise falls flat. There were many times throughout the game where I felt it was finally about to get good, but it never materialized. Then the last chapter throws everything overboard: [spoiler] the criminal out themselves undermining all the mystery; the game tries to guilt you into feeling bad for people who had done terrible things; and, for some reason, you are supposed to side with them in the end. [/spoiler]

Too many conflicted opinions to recommend this one. I believe there is a Demo; try it first.

review_text_raw:
Played only the main story - one playthrough... it was enough for me.
Too bad. Kind of a disappointment. This had a lot of potential! 
The game is meant more as a lesson of the evils of government surveillance than anything fun or playable. Unfortunately, its a very linear story to tell, and while its interesting, there is not much option for variation outside of [spoiler]a major choice at the end.[/spoiler]. Wont be getting those 4 hours back, and wont be putting in more to see alternate endings.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically a short visual novel with a unique interface and player perspective, and, as is probably obvious just from the title, a rather heavy handed message about the dangers of digital state surveillance.  You are put into the role of the low skill outsourced labor operator of an AI system for investigating various digital records and web activity to gather information about suspected criminals and terrorists and tasked with solving a bombing involving multiple fatalities which just occurred.  However, the whole thing really just ends up just being a big self-own because unlike, say Papers, Please which gently seduces you into being an instrument of state terror, Orwell tells you that's what you are, but really makes you an impartial finder of fact and has you bust some very guilty people.  On top of that, you can even have your cake and eat it too by [spoiler]simultaneously busting the politician who masterminded the system for something she's also factually guilty of, getting the whole thing shut down.[/spoiler]  Wow! I love Big Brother!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Crime investigation visual novel. It has a few game mechanics, but it mostly an interactive story. The use of the terms "episodes" in its "seasons" are accurate; you are watching, not so much playing. It is interesting, and your decisions have some effect on the story, but you are mostly following a story on rails and playing with the details. The details matter for the fate of the NPCs, but there is really just the one decision point at the end where you pick which ending you want.

If you get it in a bundle or the recent giveaway, it is not a bad time. The story has no padding, just some red herrings that you might expect in an investigative story. The use of the medium is pretty good in parts, forcing you to play the part of the ambiguous villain manipulating information and violating privacy.

I don't recommend visual novels because I do not enjoy the medium. If you would enjoy one where you get a story about government surveillance, this would be a good one for you.

Longer review at http://www.killtenrats.com/2018/09/09/orwell/

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I must say I had high expectations for this game considering the current climate of data-collection and mass surveillance. Little did I know I was in for a boring ride! 

At first, you're guided with what info can be considered relevant or not; if you make mistakes along the way your "supervior" reminds you of the mission at hand. So that's definitely a good start, especially for chapter 1. 
But then, I expected players would be gradually given more leeway as to what info to select and upload on Orwell servers. And so as the story unfolded the whole thing felt too scripted, too one-way track, and it lost its original twist. The team tries to make up for it by adding a new rule near the end; that came too late for me. 

Also, let's talk about the ending: if you're like me and you'd already figured what was really going on 2 chapters ago, it was just dragging on for too long, with all the explanations and all. Sometimes, it's best to keep it short - better, a little cryptic -, that way it leaves room for players to engage and connect the dots.
The soundtrack was nice for most of the part except when it got all ominous - a way to tell you you've come across some serious, plot-twist info: would've been nice to try and figure it out on my own.

Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game,

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Me: Starts Orwell "game"
Orwell: Insert your email address
Me: Hell no

The beginning of the "game" starts off in a typical direction where you use the power of the state to spy on these fictional characters, I felt disgusted as spying on people in general I consider to be morally reprehensible. Due to this, my first play-through was played in such a way to make progress for the state as difficult as I possibly can, it is quite an achievement that the game actually gives you the option to do this, to its credit. However, that is when issues on game progression started occurring, I would expect that it would be quite easy to proceed through the game if you started dragging and dropping everything highlighted in blue or yellow into the profiler, but if you wanted to play as a rebel then you will quite easily get stuck. 

Let me explain, to play under a persona of liberty you need to omit certain details from the system, but some of these details must be recorded to progress in the game even though associating a character with the data is against your play-through persona. This actually leads to a lot of frustration due to being "stuck" because you refuse to drag/drop a very specific keyword or phrase to advance the game, or if you somehow missed it and have to dig through all the content all over again.

There are some good points about this indoctrination drag/drop simulator.
The universe that was created including the text content, phone calls, chats and character profiles have quite a bit of effort put into them making a somewhat cohesive story.

The best part is getting Symes [spoiler]in trouble[/spoiler], well because... phuck you Symes that's why.
Yes you get an "adviser" that hovers over your shoulder making wise-crack comments and wild accusations for data that you are harvesting, Symes is the ideal state bureaucrat that everybody loves to hate.

George Orwell is spinning in his grave.
